argument: This episode surveys the theories of laughter that came before Henri Bergson's famous essay, setting up the problem his theory will later solve. Comedy and tragedy turn out to be structurally similar -- both respond to a world of complex, competing forces mostly outside anyone's control, and both aim to subvert expectations, whether by mocking the status quo or sacrificing a hero to demand change. That's part of why comedy has real political power: mocking a person or idea, as Voltaire understood, can permanently strip it of the appearance of infallibility. The three classic theories -- superiority, relief, and incongruity -- each explain some cases of laughter but each fails on others (we pity the unfortunate rather than laugh at them; some jokes build no tension; some absurd, unresolved surprises just aren't funny), leaving an unresolved tension between comedy that speaks truth to power and comedy that exists purely for absurdity's sake, a tension Bergson's own theory will try to resolve.
keyIdeas: Comedy and tragedy share a deep structural similarity: both address a problem arising from complex, competing forces mostly outside anyone's control, and both aim to subvert the viewer's expectations.

Voltaire's mockery of Rousseau illustrates comedy's political power: once people laugh at something, they stop taking it as seriously, which is why dictators fear public mockery -- it strips away the appearance of infallibility.
Bergson's approach breaks from earlier philosophers by shifting away from trying to pin down a fixed definition of 'funny' and toward examining its relation to internal human experience.

The superiority theory (we laugh because we feel superior to the butt of the joke) explains slapstick but fails to explain why we feel pity rather than amusement toward people with real health or financial problems.

The relief theory (laughter as release of built-up nervous tension, as in the mathematician joke) and the incongruity theory (laughter from violated-then-resolved expectations, as in the drywall-screws seminar example) each capture part of the picture but neither alone is sufficient, leaving philosophers with a persistent tension between comedy as truth-telling and comedy as pure absurdity.

terms.def: Bergson's term for the comedic or funny in general, which he studies through its relation to internal human experience rather than trying to define it as a fixed category.
The theory that we laugh because we feel superior to some element of the joke or situation.
The theory that laughter releases built-up nervous tension once expectations of a bad outcome are shown to be unfounded.
The theory that laughter comes from the resolution of a violated expectation, not from surprise or incongruity alone.
The unresolved disagreement over whether comedy's purpose is fundamentally political critique or purely absurd entertainment for its own sake.
